title: Pattern Lines
context: Grade 4, and the hardest topic in the chapter. An adult sees number tricks. What is actually being taught is how a pattern read off a few lines comes to be trusted: by working one more line in full. The printed exercise on the facing page leaves out one line of a multiplication pattern, so the answers it does print seem to go up by six hundred each time, and a child who carries that step on writes three wrong answers under an instruction that says not to calculate. The tool puts a missing line back, so the jumps can be seen to grow, and makes working one line in full the habit.

writeup.why: Read the pattern down a board of sums and products, carry it on, and check it by working one line in full.
writeup.look: A board of ruled lines with the answers down the right, jump labels in the margin, and a slate beside it for working one line out.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Pattern Lines' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the lines read against the lines on this phase's board, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each line is read, filled or worked, and the second is fixed at the size of the board. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The board fills the left of the working area, 560 by 400 at 64,222, ruled into six lines each 60 tall with 8 between. Each line holds one calculation, with its answer in a column down the right of the board. The numbers being multiplied or added are always written in full on every line. The jump margin stands beside the answers, 110 by 400 at 634,222. A jump label sits across the rule between every pair of neighbouring answers, as the lower answer less the upper. The growth margin stands beside that, 100 by 400 at 754,222, and writes how much each jump differs from the one above it. The slate stands at the right, 286 by 400 at 864,222. Work it out takes any line and works it in full there, digit by digit in columns, with every part of the working written. Hide or put back takes a line out of the board or slides it back into its place between its neighbours. When a line is put back, the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand, never cleared, and the line itself is reddish purple. The next line slot is the empty line under the last, and takes the child's answer. On the second phase the digit bay splits each answer on the board into two columns, its number of tens and its ones. The tens column carries on as a whole number past ninety. On the first phase the side-by-side bay runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 96 at 64,632. It holds up to three rods of counters, one above the other, the counters drawn at one size and sized so the longest rod fits. Rods can be joined end to end, doubled, tripled, and laid one along another to compare. The smaller number's rod is deep blue, the greater's amber, and a rod the child builds from them is green. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever an answer, a jump or a count is asked for, with yes and no keys under them. On the first two phases a word pad carries this board's words: consecutive, greater, middle, tens, ones and jump. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A hidden line leaves no gap. The board closes up round it exactly as the printed exercise closes up round the line it leaves out, so the trap is met here as it will be met on paper. Only the numbers being multiplied, written in full on every line, show that one was skipped, for a child who reads them.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last board the child read, with its jump labels in the margin, the line they worked in full on the slate, and any line they put back standing in its place.

phases.win: the doubled rod, one counter short, lies exactly along the two rods joined end to end
phases.does: adds the two numbers, then doubles the longer rod, takes one counter away and compares
phases.goal: two consecutive numbers make one less than twice the greater, and three make three times the middle
phases.says: Double the bigger one and take one away. Is it the same as the sum?
phases.check: Add nineteen and twenty. Then check it by doubling the greater and taking one away.
phases.feels: two rods side by side are nearly two of the bigger one, short by just one counter
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, give each group a wall calendar and have them add three dates side by side in one row. Then multiply the middle date by three and compare. Try two dates side by side against twice the later date, less one. The page calls these patterns a shortcut, but working them is no shorter than adding, so use them as patterns that always hold and to check a sum.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is the greater? Second rung, the phase's: what does doubling it and taking one away give? Third rung: the numbers are cut to four and five, and the child lays out the rods. The number keys and the word pad stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the rule names a doubling and a taking away, and the smaller number is the first one read.
wrong.move: doubles the smaller number and takes one away, getting twenty-three for twelve and thirteen.
wrong.screen: the rod of twelve is doubled and one counter taken off, and the result is laid under the two rods joined end to end, where it falls two counters short. The rod of thirteen, doubled with one counter taken off, is then laid beside it and lies exactly along. Both stay on the bay.

wrong.why: the greater number was the one to use in the rule for two, so it seems to be the one to use for three.
wrong.move: for three numbers side by side, multiplies the greatest by three, writing seventy-eight for twenty-four, twenty-five and twenty-six.
wrong.screen: three rods of the greatest are laid under the three numbers' rods, and they overhang by three counters. The longest of the three rods then gives one counter to the shortest, and three level rods of the middle number stand. The child's seventy-eight stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the side-by-side bay with two rods of counters, one a counter longer than the other
phases.soWhat: Two consecutive numbers add up to one less than twice the greater, and three add up to three times the middle one.
phases.concept: Adding numbers that sit side by side

phases.win: each column lights from top to bottom as its pattern is named
phases.does: reads down each column, says what it does, then writes the next line
phases.goal: the ones digits of the table of nine count down while the number of tens counts up
phases.says: Read down the ones. Now read down the tens. What does each one do?
phases.check: Write ten times ten, eleven times ten and twelve times ten. Say what the ones do and what the tens do.
phases.feels: one column counts down while the other counts up, and past ninety the tens just keep counting
phases.hands: Write the table of nine down the board from one nine to fourteen nines, with the tens of each answer in one colour of chalk and the ones in another. Read the ones down together, then the tens. When the tens reach nine and then ten, stop and ask how many tens one hundred and eight holds. Call ten and eleven numbers of tens, not digits, and let the class say why.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the ones digit of each answer? Second rung, the phase's: how many tens does each answer hold? Third rung: the board is cut to two lines, and the child splits each answer into tens and ones. The number keys and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: the page's commentary calls the tens column digits, and one hundred and eight has a zero where a tens digit sits.
wrong.move: reads the tens digit of one hundred and eight as zero, and decides the pattern has broken past ninety.
wrong.screen: the digit bay splits one hundred and eight into ten tens and eight ones, and the tens column reads ten under nine. The tens then carry on, eleven and twelve, with the ones counting down beside them. The child's zero stays written beside the line.

wrong.why: the table read just before went up by one ten on each line, and a pattern in one table looks like the pattern for all of them.
wrong.move: expects the tens of the table of five to go up on every line, as they do in the table of nine.
wrong.screen: the digit bay lights the tens of the table of five two lines at a time: none, one, one, two, two. The ones take turns beside them, five then zero. The child's line stays on the board with the bay's split under it.

phases.screen: the digit bay writing a times table down the board, tens in one column and ones in another
phases.soWhat: In the table of nine the ones count down while the number of tens counts up, and in the table of five the ones take turns.
phases.concept: Digits marching down a times table

phases.win: the next jump label writes itself in and the next total lands under it
phases.does: reads how much each jump grows by, finds the next jump, then writes the next total
phases.goal: when the jumps between answers grow, the next jump is found from how they grow
phases.says: Look at the jumps. How much bigger is each one than the last?
phases.check: The totals are two, six, twelve, twenty. Find the jumps, then the next total.
phases.feels: the jumps get bigger, but they get bigger in a steady way that can be carried on
phases.hands: Have the class add one, then two, then three, then four, writing each running total on a new line. Write the jump between each pair of totals in a column beside them, and the growth between the jumps in a column beside that. Ask what the growth column says, and use it to find the next jump before the next total.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what are the jumps between the totals? Second rung, the phase's: how much bigger is each jump than the last? Third rung: the board is cut to three totals, and the child writes the two jumps before anything else. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: a jump found once has always been the jump for the rest of the list, and the growth between jumps is one more thing to hold.
wrong.move: uses the last jump again, writing fourteen and eighteen after one, three, six, ten.
wrong.screen: the jump margin reads two, three and four, and the growth margin writes one and one beside them. The next jump label is left empty with its growth already written. The child's fourteen stays on the next line.

wrong.why: the growth is the newest number on the board, and adding the newest number to the last total is how every earlier line was made.
wrong.move: adds the growth to the last total instead of to the last jump, writing eleven after ten.
wrong.screen: the growth label is carried from its margin to the jump margin first, where it joins the last jump and makes the next one. Only then is the next jump carried to the total. The child's eleven stays on the next line beside it.

phases.screen: a board of running totals with the jump labels written and the next line empty
phases.soWhat: When the jumps between answers grow, find how they grow, and use that to find the next jump.

phases.win: the hidden line slides back in and the equal jumps split into jumps that grow
phases.does: guesses the next answer from the equal jumps, works that line in full on the slate, then puts the hidden line back
phases.goal: a line left out can make jumps that grow look equal, so one line is worked in full to check
phases.says: Work this line out in full. Does it agree with the guess?
phases.check: A list was copied as one, four, seven, but the two after the one was left out. Put it back. What comes after seven?
phases.feels: the jumps only looked equal, and one line worked in full was enough to show it
phases.hands: Before anyone completes the printed multiplication pattern, write its lines on the board as printed: five fives, twenty-five twenty-fives and thirty-five thirty-fives. Ask what the answers seem to do. They seem to go up by six hundred each time, only because fifteen fifteens is missing. Have the class work forty-five forty-fives in full, with the two partial products the multiplication chapter taught, and set it beside the guess. Then put fifteen fifteens back, two hundred and twenty-five, and read the jumps again: two hundred, four hundred, six hundred. They grow, and they are not equal. Do not teach a rule for multiplying a number ending in five by itself; the chapter never teaches one.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the next line come to when it is worked in full? Second rung, the phase's: do the numbers being multiplied skip one? Third rung: the board is cut to two lines with the hidden one between them, and the child puts it back. The number keys and the slate stay open.

wrong.why: every pattern met so far was carried on by its jump, and two equal jumps look like a pattern already found.
wrong.move: carries on the equal jumps of twenty-four read off three lines, and writes seventy-three for nine nines.
wrong.screen: the child's seventy-three stays on the next line, and the slate beside it lights. Nine nines is worked in full there, and the two answers stand side by side. The hide control then lights on the place between one and twenty-five. When three threes slides back in, the first jump label is rewritten where it stands as eight and sixteen, and the jumps are seen to grow.

wrong.why: the jumps were equal and looked settled, and a long piece of working feels easier to get wrong than a pattern.
wrong.move: works the line in full, gets a different answer from the guess, and decides the working must be the slip.
wrong.screen: the slate works the line again with every part of the working written in its column, and lands on the same answer. The guess and the worked line stand together on the board. The numbers being multiplied are then read down the board aloud, one, five, seven, and the skipped three is found between them.

phases.screen: a board with one line hidden, its answers seeming to go up by equal jumps, and the slate waiting
phases.soWhat: A line left out can make jumps that grow look equal, so a pattern read off a few lines is checked by working one line in full.
phases.concept: A missing line can hide the pattern

writeup.delight: The first phase, when three numbers side by side are laid out as rods. The longest rod gives up its last counter, which walks across and joins the end of the shortest. The three rods then stand level, each as long as the middle one, and the three together are seen to make three of the middle number. Lay out any three numbers in a row and it runs again, as often as a finger likes. Nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the side-by-side bay holds two rods of counters, one a counter longer than the other, with the board above it showing their sum as one line. On the second the digit bay has split a times table down the board into tens and ones, with the next line empty. On the third a board of running totals stands with its jump labels written and the next line empty. On the fourth a board stands with one line already hidden, its answers seeming to go up by equal jumps, and the slate waiting clean. The running count at the top left holds the lines read against the lines on this phase's board, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once, the longer rod or the first ones digit or the last jump label or the next empty line. It gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the answers do. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any board of sums or products, with the jump labels, the digit bay, the slate and the hide control all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on sums of consecutive numbers, the digits of the tables of five, nine and ten, totals whose jumps grow, and a pattern checked by working one line in full.
voiceLines: A board of sums, one to a line. Read down the answers before you write.
Double the bigger one and take one away. Is it the same as the sum?
Read down the ones. Now read down the tens. What does each one do?
Look at the jumps. How much bigger is each one than the last?
Work this line out in full. Does it agree with the guess?
Another board. Look at the jump between every pair of answers.
Free play. Any board, with the jumps, the slate and the hide control open.
Work that line out in full on the slate, then read the jumps again.
Every board read, and every guess checked against a line worked in full.

observations.why: Two numbers side by side make the greater one twice over, with one counter missing from the smaller.
observations.soWhat: Two consecutive numbers add up to one less than twice the greater, and working it is a way to check a sum.
observations.observe: The doubled rod, one counter short, lay exactly along the two rods joined end to end.

observations.why: The column counts how many tens the answer holds, and one hundred and eight holds ten of them.
observations.soWhat: Ten and eleven are numbers of tens, not digits, so the pattern carries on unbroken.
observations.observe: Past ninety the tens column kept counting, nine, ten, eleven, and never went back to zero.

observations.why: Each jump was the same amount bigger than the jump before it.
observations.soWhat: When the jumps grow, find how they grow, and the next jump comes from that.
observations.observe: The growth margin read the same all the way down while the jumps kept getting bigger.

observations.why: The equal jumps came from the missing line, not from the pattern.
observations.soWhat: A pattern read off a few lines is checked by working one line in full.
observations.observe: Putting the hidden line back split one of two equal jumps into two smaller jumps that grew.

source_tool.description: A board of ruled lines fills the stage, one calculation to a line, with the answers down the right. Between every pair of neighbouring answers a jump label sits in the margin, filled by taking one answer from the next, so the child can see whether the answers go up by equal jumps or by jumps that grow, and a second margin beside it labels how much each jump grows by. A side-by-side bay sets consecutive numbers out as rods of counters, so two numbers in a row can be seen to make twice the greater with one counter short, and three in a row to make three rods the size of the middle one. A digit bay writes a times table down the board with each answer split into its number of tens and its ones, so the ones of the table of nine can be read counting down while the tens count up, and past ninety the tens column carries on as a number of tens rather than a single digit. A work it out control takes any one line and works it in full on a slate beside the board, so a pattern read off a few lines is checked against a line actually worked. A line can be hidden or put back, and when a line is put back the jump labels either side of it are rewritten, so equal-looking jumps that came from a missing line are seen to split into jumps that grow.
source_tool.art_direction: A ruled board of sums, slate beside / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip of picture cells, a paper arrow on a dial, stepping stones with jump arcs between them, counters that pair up, a tower of boxes each resting on two below, two rings of letters that turn, a ruled board of sums with a slate beside it, and a bench of dotted paper with a tray of tiles.
A repeating group is always shown whole. When a bracket is drawn over it, every copy of it along the row is lit at once, and a copy that does not match is left unlit rather than hidden.

Every step in a series is drawn as an arc from one term to the next with its label on the arc, never as a bare number between two terms, so the step between every pair of neighbours can be read, not only the first.
A counting-down track has a zero stone at its left end and nothing beyond it. No track, board or list is ever drawn running on past zero.

Every box of a number tower rests visibly on exactly two boxes below it, and the operation sign is drawn between each pair of neighbours in every row, so a tower that keeps to one operation shows the same sign all the way up.
The alphabet is always drawn round a circle, twenty-six letters evenly spaced, so the last letter sits beside the first and no letter ever falls off an end.
A line put back into a board is drawn sliding into its place between its neighbours, and the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand, never cleared.

Tiles are drawn at true relative size, edge to edge where they touch, never overlapping unless the frame is showing an overlap on purpose, and a circle is never squeezed to close a gap. A tile drawn taller than it is wide is never called a square.
A shape, a term or a box is told apart by its label or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a shape, a term, a box, a letter or a tile the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Whatever the stage hands over, a printed term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter of a message and a tile already laid, is deep blue, and so is the first member of a repeating group. The second member of a repeating group, and a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself, a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, the operation sign between two boxes and the shift a key makes from a letter to its partner, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is the rule cannot afford a frame where the step has to be hunted for. Whatever the rule makes, a next term, a box built from the two below it, a coded or decoded letter, a tile carried on and a tick on the can do list, is green. Whatever the child is asked to notice, a box that breaks the tower's operation, a space with tiles closed round it, a part where two tiles lie on top of each other, a counter left without a partner and a missing line put back on a board, is reddish purple. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome, and the outer edge of a tiled patch is traced in that plain line and never filled, because it is where the tiling stops and not a gap. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box and never a faded copy of its answer. All of that holds in greyscale, because a jump label sits on its own arc, a broken box keeps its light on after the check has moved past it, a closed-in gap is filled while the outer edge is only outlined, and a leftover counter stands apart from the pairs.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Work that line out in full on the slate, then read the jumps again.
voice.onNext: Another board. Look at the jump between every pair of answers.
voice.opening: A board of sums, one to a line. Read down the answers before you write.
voice.onFinish: Every board read, and every guess checked against a line worked in full.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any board, with the jumps, the slate and the hide control open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Adding numbers that sit side by side
Digits marching down a times table
A missing line can hide the pattern

placement.where: After three dates side by side on a wall calendar have been added and checked against three times the middle one, and before the printed patterns are completed. The tool is what puts a missing line back into a board and rewrites the jumps either side of it, which a printed page cannot do.

answer_key.rule: Numbers that sit side by side in counting are consecutive. Two consecutive numbers add up to one less than twice the greater, and three add up to three times the middle one. Working either pattern is no shorter than adding, so it is used as a pattern that always holds and as a way to check a sum. In the table of five the ones digit takes turns, five then zero. In the table of nine the ones digit counts down from nine to zero while the number of tens counts up, and past ninety the number of tens carries on, ten tens in one hundred and eight and eleven in one hundred and seventeen. In the table of ten the ones digit is always zero and the number of tens is the number being multiplied. When the answers down a board go up by jumps that grow, find how the jumps grow and carry that on. A pattern read off a few lines is checked by working one line in full, and a line left out can make jumps that grow look equal.
answer_key.wrong: The line in question is worked in full on the slate beside the board, and the jump labels in the margin are rewritten from the worked answer, so the guess and the worked line stand on the board together. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Twice the greater number is 13 x 2 = 26, and one less than that is 25.
The two answers match. The pattern saves no work, but it is a way to check the sum.
items.answer: Both give 25, because two numbers side by side add up to one less than twice the greater
items.question: Add 12 and 13. Then double 13 and take away 1. What do you notice?
items.checkpoint: Two numbers side by side add up to one less than twice the greater.
items.misconception: Doubling the smaller number instead of the greater, and getting 24.

steps: Read the ones: 9, 8, 7, 6, one less each time.
Count the tens: 99 has nine tens, 108 has ten, 117 has eleven and 126 has twelve, one more each time.
items.answer: 99, 108, 117 and 126. The ones digits count down 9, 8, 7, 6, and the number of tens counts up 9, 10, 11, 12
items.question: Write 11 x 9, 12 x 9, 13 x 9 and 14 x 9. What do the ones digits do, and what does the number of tens do?
items.checkpoint: Past ninety, count the number of tens, because ten tens or more is not a single digit.
items.misconception: Reading the tens digit of 108 as 0 and deciding that the pattern has broken.

steps: The jumps between the totals are 2, 3 and 4.
Each jump is one more than the jump before, so the next jumps are 5 and 6.
items.question: The totals 1, 3, 6, 10 come from adding 1, then 2, then 3, then 4. What are the next two totals?
items.checkpoint: When the jumps grow, find how they grow and carry that on.
items.misconception: Using the last jump, 4, again, and writing 14 and 18.

steps: Work the next line in full: 9 x 9 = 81, not 73, so the equal jumps gave a wrong answer.
The line 3 x 3 = 9 was left out. Put it back and the answers are 1, 9, 25, 49.
The jumps are 8, 16, 24 and then 32. They grow and are not equal, and 49 + 32 = 81.
items.answer: No. 9 x 9 = 81. The line 3 x 3 = 9 is missing, and with it put back the jumps are 8, 16 and 24, so the next jump is 32
items.question: A board shows 1 x 1 = 1, 5 x 5 = 25 and 7 x 7 = 49. The answers seem to go up by 24 and 24. Is 9 x 9 equal to 73?
items.checkpoint: A pattern read off a few lines is checked by working one line in full.
items.misconception: Carrying on the equal jumps of 24 without noticing that a line is missing.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Add 24, 25 and 26. Then multiply the middle number by 3. Do the two answers match?
Check the sum 30 + 31 = 61 by doubling the greater number and taking one away.
items.final_answer: 31 x 2 = 62, and one less is 61, so the sum is right

items.question: Write 5 x 11, 5 x 12, 5 x 13 and 5 x 14. What do the ones digits do?
items.final_answer: 55, 60, 65 and 70. The ones digits take turns, 5 then 0

items.question: Find the pattern in 16 x 10, 17 x 10 and 18 x 10.
items.final_answer: 160, 170 and 180. The ones digit is always 0, and the number of tens is the number multiplied by ten: 16, 17 and 18

items.question: 3 + 6 = 9 and 3 + 6 + 9 = 18. What are 3 + 6 + 9 + 12 and 3 + 6 + 9 + 12 + 15?
items.final_answer: 30 and 45. The totals 3, 9, 18, 30 and 45 jump by 6, 9, 12 and 15, growing by three each time

items.question: 5 x 5 = 25, 6 x 6 = 36 and 7 x 7 = 49. Do the answers go up by equal jumps? What is 8 x 8?
items.final_answer: No. The jumps are 11 and 13, growing by two, so the next jump is 15 and 8 x 8 = 64

items.question: 2 = 2; 2 + 22 = 24; 2 + 22 + 222 = 246; 2 + 22 + 222 + 2222 = 2468. A guess says the next answer is 246810. Work 2468 + 22222 in full. Is the guess right?
items.final_answer: No, the guess is wrong. 2468 + 22222 = 24690, so working one line in full shows where the digit pattern stops

items.question: A list was copied as 4, 10, 16, and the next number was guessed as 22. But 6 had been left out between 4 and 10. Put it back. What really comes after 16?
items.final_answer: 24. The full list is 4, 6, 10, 16, with jumps 2, 4 and 6, so the next jump is 8. The equal jumps of 6 came from the missing number, and 22 is wrong

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds one calculation to a line with the answers down the right
write the jump between each pair of neighbouring answers
writes how much each jump grows by
sets consecutive numbers out as rods of counters
splits each answer of a times table into its tens and its ones
works any one line in full on a slate beside the board
takes a line out of the board or slides it back in
takes the child's answer for the next line down

teaching_notes: Add three dates side by side on a wall calendar before the tool is opened, and check the total against three times the middle date. The page calls its two adding patterns a shortcut, but working them is no shorter than adding, so use them as patterns that always hold and as a way to check a sum. In the table of nine, past ninety, talk about the number of tens, nine in ninety-nine and ten in one hundred and eight; the page's commentary calls ten and eleven digits, and they are not. Then the exercise on the facing page. Its multiplication pattern prints five fives, twenty-five twenty-fives and thirty-five thirty-fives, and leaves out fifteen fifteens. With that line missing, the three printed answers seem to go up by six hundred each time, and a child who carries that step on writes three wrong answers, while the instruction forbids the calculation that would show it. Before anyone completes it, have the class work one line in full, forty-five forty-fives, with the two partial products the multiplication chapter taught, and compare it with the guess. Then put fifteen fifteens back, two hundred and twenty-five, and read the jumps again: two hundred, four hundred, six hundred. They grow, and they are not equal. Do not teach a rule for multiplying a number ending in five by itself. The chapter never teaches one, and supplying it would stop this being a plan for this chapter.
generation_prompt: Build a pattern board tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A board of ruled lines fills most of the working area, one calculation written to a line with its answer in a column down the right. In a margin beside the answers a jump label sits between every pair of neighbouring answers showing their difference, and a second margin beside that shows how much each jump differs from the one above it. A side-by-side bay sets two or three consecutive numbers out as horizontal rods of counters that can be joined end to end, doubled or tripled and compared. A digit bay writes a times table down the board with each answer split into a column for its number of tens and a column for its ones, the tens column carrying on as a whole number past ninety. A work it out control takes any line and works it in full, digit by digit in columns, on a slate beside the board. A hide or put back control removes a line or slides it back into its place between its neighbours, and the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand. A next line slot takes the child's answer for the line below the last. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read down the answers. Look at the jump between each pair. If the jumps grow, find how they grow. Work one line out in full to check. Put back any line that is missing.
